messages.subject: Forward Sampling Examples

Peter,

Do you have any good examples of a model with forward sampling?  Additionally, a list of the implemented random variables would be handy (is there a branch where they have been doc'd?).

Thanks.

-Mike

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Forward Sampling Examples
messages.body_plain:
I'm referring to generating random quantities in the "generated quantities" block, a la posterior predictive checking.  In other words is this the general procedure?

parameters {
  real mu;
}

model {
  mu ~ normal(0, 1);
}

generated_quantities {
  real nu;
  nu ~ normal_rng(mu, 1);
}

And have all of the distributions in Stan been rng'd, or are there still a few exceptions?

messages.subject: Re: Explicit template instantiation -- help?
messages.body_plain:
Looks like forward declaring a static const int within a class doesn't work either.

On Thu, Aug 1, 2013 at 1:10 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> I'm stumped. I'm trying to forward declare a struct with an enum inside. Something like the stuff in src/stan/meta/traits.hpp: is_constant is one of the examples.
>
> Am I not allowed to forward declare a struct / class if it has a public enum inside? I've been searching the web for an answer on this for a while, but I think I haven't hit the search right keywords yet.
>
> Here's a simple example (adapted from wiki's metatemplate programming entry):
>
> --------------------------
>
> #include <gtest/gtest.h>
>
> template <int N>
> struct Factorial {
>   enum { value = N * Factorial<N - 1>::value };
> };
>
> template <>
> struct Factorial<0> {
>     enum { value = 1 };
> };
>
> TEST(test, factorial) {
>   const int x = Factorial<4>::value; // == 24
>   const int y = Factorial<0>::value; // == 1
>
>   EXPECT_EQ(24, x);
>   EXPECT_EQ(1, y);
> }
>
> --------------------------
>
> That works fine.
>
>
>
>
>
> I can split the header and definition to something like:
>
> --------------------------
> header: factorial.hpp
>
> template <int N>
> struct Factorial;
>
> --------------------------
>
> definition: factorial_def.hpp
>
> template <int N>
> struct Factorial {
>   enum { value = N * Factorial<N - 1>::value };
> };
>
> template <>
> struct Factorial<0> {
>     enum { value = 1 };
> };
>
> --------------------------
> test file:
>
> #include <gtest/gtest.h>
> #include <factorial_def.hpp>
>
> TEST(test, factorial) {
>   const int x = Factorial<4>::value; // == 24
>   const int y = Factorial<0>::value; // == 1
>
>   EXPECT_EQ(24, x);
>   EXPECT_EQ(1, y);
> }
>
> --------------------------
>
> And that works fine.
>
>
>
>
>
> The next step is where things break down. I want my test to look like:
> --------------------------
> test file:
>
> #include <gtest/gtest.h>
> #include <factorial.hpp>
>
> TEST(test, factorial) {
>   const int x = Factorial<4>::value; // == 24
>   const int y = Factorial<0>::value; // == 1
>
>   EXPECT_EQ(24, x);
>   EXPECT_EQ(1, y);
> }
> --------------------------
>
> explicit template instantiation file: factorial_inst.cpp
>
> #include <factorial_def.hpp>
>
> template struct Factorial<4>;
> template struct Factorial<1>;
>
> --------------------------
>
>
> header and definition are left alone.
>
>
>
> The error I run into while trying to compile the test is this:
>
> src/test/tmp_test.cpp:11:17: error: implicit instantiation of undefined template 'Factorial<4>'
>   const int x = Factorial<4>::value; // == 24
>                 ^
> src/stan/factorial.hpp:5:8: note: template is declared here
> struct Factorial;
>        ^
> src/test/tmp_test.cpp:12:17: error: implicit instantiation of undefined template 'Factorial<0>'
>   const int y = Factorial<0>::value; // == 1
>                 ^
> src/stan/factorial.hpp:5:8: note: template is declared here
> struct Factorial;
>        ^
>
>
> Anyone know how to make this work? Or is there a way to restructure our traits classes to break this apart? I feel like I'll need the trick later on even if I were to ignore our traits classes, but I could be wrong.
>
>
>
> Daniel
>
>
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Explicit template instantiation -- help?
messages.body_plain:
I found enum didn't work, which is why some
of the flags inside of ast.hpp are done with
int.  These aren't members of a class, though,
just namespace level enums.

You do declare member variables of a class in
the header because the declaration needs that
information to size the variable.

- Bob

is set up in BUGS, it calls things like

either. Is there another way to do this or would it be worth adding
multi_normal for row_vectors y and mu?

The inverse() function should pretty much never be used, since it neither utilizes the fact that a covariance matrix is positive definite nor does a good job at preserving positive definiteness when the matrix is numerically near singular.

messages.body_plain:
On 8/2/13 6:09 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> With 2x2 we can use the notation with rho etc..  With more than 2x2 we should be using priors directly on the cov matrix.
> A
>
> On Aug 2, 2013, at 12:13 PM, Peter Li wrote:
>
>> I'm currently working on the sesame street model (ARM Ch23.4) and it involves fitting a multivariate normal distribution. However, the way it is set up in BUGS, it calls things like
>>
>>   ag[j,1:2] ~ dmnorm (mu.ag <http://mu.ag>[1:2],Tau.ag[1:2,1:2])

>>
>> where ag is a matrix[N,2]. I've tried using temp variables, but I've found that it gets too messy since I can't assign variables in the model block (i.e. a <- blah). However, a potential work around is to call it as
>>
>> ag[j] ~ multi_normal(mu_ag,Tau_ag)
>>
>> where ag[j] and mu_ag are both row vectors, but this isn't supported either. Is there another way to do this or would it be worth adding multi_normal for row_vectors y and mu?

The best approach is this:

   vector[2] ag[N];

   vector[2] mu_ag;

   cov_matrix[2] Tau_ag;

That way ag[n] is a vector, and everything should match the
signature.

The other way you could've done it is with an explicit transpose,
because ag[n]' is a vector if ag is a matrix[N,2].

We've been meaning to generalize the way multi_normal works
for ages but haven't gotten around to it yet.

- Bob

On Saturday, August 3, 2013 4:36:20 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On 8/3/13 4:20 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>
> > If Ross / Dan / whomever are up for it, packaging for Debian would be really beneficial. It would mean Stan gets a lot
> > of testing on non-Intel platforms, facilitate the python integration, etc.
>
> That would be great.

Also, it would re-open the possibility of getting Stan-related packages onto CRAN.

> How does it facilitate Python integration?  (I'm pretty much
> completely ignorant about Python and Linux packaging.)

The Pystan repo is like RStan in that it embeds its dependencies. If there were Stan-related Debian packages, then it would be pretty easy to make a tiny python-pystan Debian package that also used the system libraries. It doesn't make anything easier on Mac or Windows.

> > It just means doing a lot of things the
> > Debian way instead of the wrong way.
>
> Could you be more specific?  I know we've talked before about
> lib and compiler dependencies.

Debian is as much a religion as it is a Linux distribution. But I would say that three of the packaging principles are

-- Don't embed dependencies on other software
-- Make version requirements as lenient as possible
-- Separate the library from the headers from the binaries from the test-suite, etc.

(R)Stan is pretty much the opposite of that, but it wouldn't be that hard to have a Debian git branch that facilitated doing things the way Debian requires them.

Ben

messages.subject: increment_log_prob plan
messages.body_plain:
I went with the function-like syntax:

   increment_log_prob(e);

The expression e must be assignable to real.

As Marcus suggested, the underlying implementation uses
an accumulator that returns a sum() at the end.  Should be
much faster than incremental summations, each of which required
playing with memory and a virtual function call.

The use of lp__ is discouraged by having it print a warning.
The warning indicates that it will go away in the future and
that increment_log_prob() should be used instead.

I replaced all uses of lp__ in the doc and in the example
models with increment_log_prob().  I also replaced all the
mentions of lp__ in the text of the doc.

I added a new section to the doc for increment_log_prob().
I added a small subsection in that section about lp__ mentioning
that it's deprecated.

We could just get rid of it instead of deprecating it,
but I thought this way would be gentler for the users.

Any other suggestions?

- Bob

messages.subject: all vs. trimmed Boost & Eigen
messages.body_plain:
Can we take this discussion over to stan-dev?

More below.

On 8/5/13 9:46 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

 > The cost of having
> hundreds of MB of unused headers was deemed less than the cost of running a one-line bcp command.

I don't have a problem with cutting down Boost or Eigen in our
official releases.

I made a similar comment about cutting down the Eigen contributed
code and I seem to recall the consensus was that I should leave it
intact.

I recall the following concerns about trimming Boost and Eigen:

1.  Users might try to use it as their Boost or Eigen distribution
and be disappointed that it's incomplete.

2.  We might try to use it as our Boost or Eigen distribution during
development and not have everything we need when we want to use a new
feature.

3.  Something might go wrong in the include tool, especially w.r.t.
templates.

4.  Adding another tool adds complexity to our build process.

I'm not at all worried about (1).

As to (2), what should we do with our Git repository?

As to (3), Jiqiang seems to have evertyhing working for RStan.

For (4), I think it may be worth it to cut down our distribution size.
Also as we (or maybe just I) get more comfortable with all the other
tools, the decision to add a new one gets cheaper.  And new developers
may be insulated from these issues if the solution to (2)'s simple
enough.

One thing that's nice about the way we have things set up now is that
the release just mirrors the GitHub structure and the libs mirror their
distributions, so it's very conceptually simple.  I value conceptual
simplicity very highly in software, but there are tradeoffs.

I'm also assuming their licenses are OK with less-than-complete
redistributions.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, August 5, 2013 11:20:13 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I made a similar comment about cutting down the Eigen contributed
> code and I seem to recall the consensus was that I should leave it
> intact.

Eigen is more challenging because there is no tool like bcp to sort out the dependencies. Also, Eigen is smaller so there is less to gain. But it is still probably a good idea in principle.

> I recall the following concerns about trimming Boost and Eigen:
>
> 1.  Users might try to use it as their Boost or Eigen distribution
> and be disappointed that it's incomplete.

Such people probably download Boost and Eigen from upstream or easily could.

> 2.  We might try to use it as our Boost or Eigen distribution during
> development and not have everything we need when we want to use a new
> feature.

Then we just have to add some headers back. Both Boost and Eigen have git repos.

> 3.  Something might go wrong in the include tool, especially w.r.t.
> templates.

Just need to run the tests before merging the pull request that deletes stuff.

> 4.  Adding another tool adds complexity to our build process.

I think we need to cut from the repo, and at that point the build process is the same.

>
> One thing that's nice about the way we have things set up now is that
> the release just mirrors the GitHub structure and the libs mirror their
> distributions, so it's very conceptually simple.  I value conceptual
> simplicity very highly in software, but there are tradeoffs.

The directory would have the same structure, just fewer subdirectories and possibly fewer files within the subdirectories.

> I'm also assuming their licenses are OK with less-than-complete
> redistributions.

Yes.

Just do

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ mkdir /tmp/boost_1.54.0
goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ export STAN_HOME=/opt/stan
goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ find ${STAN_HOME}/src -name \*\.\[ch]pp -exec bcp --scan --boost=${STAN_HOME}/lib/boost_1.54.0 '{}' /tmp/boost_1.54.0/ \; &> /tmp/boost_1.54.0/bcp.log
goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ make CC=clang++ BOOST=/tmp/boost_1.54.0 -j9 test-headers && echo "boost working"

If that works, it should be safe to then do

git checkout develop
git checkout -b feature/less_boost
git rm -rf lib/boost_1.54.0
mv /tmp/boost_1.54.0 lib
rm lib/boost_1.54.0/bcp.log
git add lib
git commit -m "trim boost"

Ben

messages.subject: Stan 2.0 command-line structure
messages.body_plain:
I hadn't quite realized the extent to which Michael has been
innovating on the command-line front in the feature/arg_refactor
branch.  I still haven't quite put my head around all the dependencies
entailed by the help or the doc.

I think it would be helpful to have more examples with more
config of command-line calls in the manual.

I like the way the help works.  Calling

   ./my-model help

prints out a list of subcommands (and any global options)
and then

   ./my-model sample help

does what I expect in printing out the options appropriate
for sample.  It would help to have more detail here --- I was
hoping for enough to let me configure the command, not just
a list of keys without values.  This forces the user to go back
to help-all and then try to navigate that maze.

Ideally, we'd have the same behavior from

   ./my-model nuts help

Note that I wrote this without "sample".  And that "help" comes
last.  The idea is that you invoke the help option of the
subcommand nuts.  But I don't see how to make this fly.

In general, is there a way to make subcommands imply their super-commands?
I'd rather not have to write

   ./my-model sample nuts ...

But this doesn't work either, as apparently nuts needs some kind
of key.  So I dug through the doc and played with a sample model
and realized I needed to do this:

./my-model sample algorithm=hmc engine=nuts

It's not so bad.  But why no "--" before keys?  Is this kosher with
the command-lines of the world?  I've just followed what I've seen in
other software like a good monkey (of the "monkey see, monkey do" species).

I don't have a better suggestion than "algorithm" (hmc) vs. "engine" (nuts).
It's a bit arbitrary because NUTS is a kind of HMC algorithm, which
in turn is a kind of Metropolis algorithm, which in turn is a kind of MCMC
algorithm.  So it's algorithms (or engines if we want to go steam punk)
all the way down.

This brings up the issue that the commands and options are not in
a strict hierarchy.  It seems like the random options, for instance,
get used across subcommands.   Then there's mass matrix adaptation for HMC,
which is very much like covariance adaptation for Metropolis, but in other
ways it's very different.

I'm still cogitating on this, but it may be
that there's no better way in general to do it than Michael
came up with.  You can think about it as being all key=value, with
lots of consistency checking implied by the "hierarchy".

- Bob

Can't be done in the current framework since we allow subcommands to be resused (for example, hmc, nesterov, and bfgs all use arg_stepsize to configure their stepsize) so the mapping from subcommand to command isn't one-to-one.  We could have help completely ignore the hierarchy and give the arguments print methods of their own, but then we wouldn't be able to print info about related arguments since that requires the hierarchy.

> In general, is there a way to make subcommands imply their super-commands?
> I'd rather not have to write
>
>   ./my-model sample nuts ...
>
> But this doesn't work either, as apparently nuts needs some kind
> of key.  So I dug through the doc and played with a sample model
> and realized I needed to do this:
>

Right, there's no argument called "nuts" -- it's just a value.  We could add "shortcuts" that would expand "nuts" into the proper command, if necessary.

> It's not so bad.  But why no "--" before keys?  Is this kosher with
> the command-lines of the world?  I've just followed what I've seen in
> other software like a good monkey (of the "monkey see, monkey do" species).

It's cleaner.  I think Dan made an executive decision at some point.

> I don't have a better suggestion than "algorithm" (hmc) vs. "engine" (nuts).
> It's a bit arbitrary because NUTS is a kind of HMC algorithm, which
> in turn is a kind of Metropolis algorithm, which in turn is a kind of MCMC
> algorithm.  So it's algorithms (or engines if we want to go steam punk)
> all the way down.

Yeah, the hierarchy is in no way unique but this classification provided the least reuse of arguments.  Also, we really should rename "metropolis" to "rw_metropolis" (Random-Walk Metropolis) before we implement it.

> This brings up the issue that the commands and options are not in
> a strict hierarchy.  It seems like the random options, for instance,
> get used across subcommands.   Then there's mass matrix adaptation for HMC,
> which is very much like covariance adaptation for Metropolis, but in other
> ways it's very different.

The design allows argument implementations to be resued, but then they become unique in the hierarchy; this avoids code duplication while also respecting the hierarchy.  For example, we can have different adaptation options for RWM and HMC but not have to rewrite the arguments that they share.

>
> I'm still cogitating on this, but it may be
> that there's no better way in general to do it than Michael
> came up with.  You can think about it as being all key=value, with
> lots of consistency checking implied by the "hierarchy".

It's slightly more general.  There are three kinds of arguments:

1) valued arguments
2) unvalued arguments

Valued arguments, which break down into lists arguments and singleton arguments, follow the key=value format.

Unvalued arguments have no value.  These break down into categorical arguments (for example, adapt which just leads into all of the adaptation options) and flags that specify a choice (these are used like enums, for example in the possible metrics for HMC).

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, August 7, 2013 11:04:17 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> It's not so bad.  But why no "--" before keys?  Is this kosher with
> the command-lines of the world?  I've just followed what I've seen in
> other software like a good monkey (of the "monkey see, monkey do" species).

The de facto way of doing things is with "short" and "long" dashes. The one dash version means that you just type a space and then the value after like

tail -n 5 TO-DO.txt

and the two dash version uses an equal sign to do the equivalent thing

tail --lines=5 TO-DO.txt

Usually if something is not proceeded by any dashes, it is considered data, as in TO-DO.txt.

Since command-line Stan is disproportionally used by people who do things via the command-line, I think we should stick with the conventions.

Ben

messages.subject: removing rejecting warning
messages.body_plain:
I propose we just remove the rejection warning message
altogether in 2.0.

There are two cases where it comes up:

1.  Early in adaptation and occassionally during sampling
when step sizes are too large.

2.  During inititalization or during sampling when the
parameters don't have the correct constraints specified.

The warning message seems to both confuse users and undermine
their trust in their own models and Stan as a sampler.  So I
think it's better if we just get rid of it.

In case (2), the fact that samples continue to be rejected
will provide some clue.

Another issue is that only some of our functions throw these
execptions --- others just return NaN silently.

-Bob

messages.subject: fwd & rev namespaces?
messages.body_plain:
On 8/8/13 5:55 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
> Thanks. This email helps a lot.
>
> On Wed, Aug 7, 2013 at 6:29 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
>
>     I'm still not sure if it makes sense to introduce fwd and
>     rev namespaces.  I understand now that we need to define
>     their ops in a namespace where we can use argument-dependent
>     lookup OR we need to make sure all of the fwd and rev versions
>     are proper specializations rather than overloads so that we
>     can import just the stan::math version.
>
>
> Hmmm. I don't think my head is fully around that paragraph. I think if we really want the auto diff library to exist on
> its own, I would think that it'd be good to include either the reverse header, the forward header, or both and just use
> the stan::math namespace. I'm not sure I'm convinced about the namespace thing, though.

The question is how do we pick up the auto-diff versions?

If they're in their own namespace, such as stan::agrad, then
the right versions get picked up by argument-dependent lookup.

Suppose foo is defined in stan::math::foo and we try to define:

    template <typename T>
    T two_foo(const T& x) {
      using stan::math::foo;
      return 2 * foo(x);
    }

So we only have a using statement for stan::math.  But if
foo(stan::agrad::var) is defined in the stan::agrad
namespace, then  argument-dependent lookup will bring in the
right version of foo will be used for two_foo.

This approach also works for std::exp, defined in std namespace.

For our own functions, we could alternatively define the agrad::fwd
version of foo in the stan::math namespace and then use template
specializations or overloading.  Template specializations are
problematic for functions without C++-11.

So I think we should just continue to define agrad versions of
functions in the agrad namespace.  It's consistent with what we
have to do with std:: functions.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stan 2.0 command-line structure
messages.body_plain:
Looks like I missed a whole bunch of conversations while I had my head deep in code. I'm going to try to pick things out of past conversations and hopefully the message comes out coherent enough.

On Aug 7, 2013, at 7:38 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Braces or a suffix'd colon would still be possible,
>
> adapt={mu=5 eta=8 t0=2...}
> --algorithm=hmc={metric=unit_e stepsize=0.1…}
>
> Although that would require some nontrivial parsing work.

A couple points here:
- Braces are a bad idea, I think. I think the shell will do stuff with braces before it enters our program. I think users might be able to get it to us if they quoted or escaped it somehow, but I think it's really not the best option for us.
- Regarding colon: it will be nontrivial parsing work. I would rather not introduce more complexity in our wrapper than necessary. I would prefer to not maintain complex logic / code here.

On Aug 7, 2013, at 11:22 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> It's not so bad.  But why no "--" before keys?  Is this kosher with
> the command-lines of the world?  I've just followed what I've seen in
> other software like a good monkey (of the "monkey see, monkey do" species).
>
> It's cleaner.  I think Dan made an executive decision at some point.

On Aug 7, 2013, at 6:45 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > I think we should stick
>> with the conventions.
>
> I agree.  This doesn't seem like the place to innovate.
>
> I prefer the verbose names with -- and =, which not
> coincidentally matches the way it was done in 1.0.

Yes, I think I made that call a while ago, but I was thinking along the lines of git subcommands. I didn't think it through. We have a lot more key, value pairs that we deal with.

And yes, I don't want to innovate here. Unfortunately, I don't think there's a good standard. I know it's a little late, but if we're trying to do something more standard, what about using the Boost Program_options library? http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_54_0/doc/html/program_options.html

Unfortunately, it's NOT header only. But if it makes sense to use it, I'll figure it out unless someone else volunteers.

On Aug 8, 2013, at 4:15 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On 8/7/13 7:24 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>>> Eventually, it might be nice to have the inverse relations.
>>> That is,
>>>
>>>  stepsize -> hmc | nesterov | bfgs
>>>
>>> so that if someone enters stepsize and not an appropriate subcommand,
>>> we can be more informative.
>>
>> What we could do is search through the hierarchy for all occurrences and show the possible paths.
>>

> ...

>>> Do we really need to say "adapt" or "random"?  It introduces
>>> order constraints and seems very clunky.  I'd rather write
>>> adapt_foo for all of its features if we had to and perhaps reuse
>>> the code at a slightly higher level than the names of the args.
>>
>> Personally I like the ability to have categorical arguments like this.  For one, it avoids having to rewrite the category name over and over

> > again (imagine the user frustration of having to type adapt_mu=5 adapt_eta=8 adapt_t0=2…).

> > We could add braces adapt={ mu=5 eta=8 t0=2 } but then we'd have to deal with
> > closure checking.  Or perhaps just add a trailing colon?  adapt: mu=5 eta=8 t0=2?
>
> I'm not saying it's a bad idea.  Just that it's unusual,
> and hence provides a bit of a learning curve.  So
> and I'm not sure this is where we want to innovate.

> ...

> What do others think here?  I could be convinced to innovate
> on the command line.  Someone has to do it some time.

I know, there was a lot of discussion here. What I would like is consistency. And hopefully we have enough foresight to provide consistency in the command line interface for at least a few releases. I think we're on the right path.

One thing I did want to mention is that the combinatorics haven't overwhelmed us yet. I still think with the number of options we have for v2.0, we can still have a "flat" subcommand structure even though it acts and feels hierarchical. Or vice versa. For printing help, we can even do what git does and have each subcommand have a char* array which we just pipe to output.

I'll get to the point: we should focus on designing the interaction on the command line.

With that said, I can roll with anything that's consistent, whether that's standard or innovative. Mike's done enough for me to be ok with the options, but if anyone has strong opinions, I'll gladly defer.

> What we probably really need is some kind of config file.
> I took a quick poll.   I hate config files, Mitzi loves them :-)

I think it makes sense to have config files eventually.

>>

I think so. I think "adapt" is the subcommand and "mu=5 eta=8 t0=2" are arguments. If I'm to understand correctly, the standard way to do this is to type:
"adapt --mu=5 --eta=8 --t0=2"
or is it:
"adapt --mu 5 --eta 8 --t0 2"
?

And should something like this be standard too?

That would be the single dash abbreviated form. Spaces wouldn't work here.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stan 2.0 command-line structure
messages.body_plain:
> And should something like this be standard too?
> "adapt -m=5 -e=8 -t=2"
> That would be the single dash abbreviated form. Spaces wouldn't work here.

The expected standard would be
"adapt -m 5 -e 8 -t 2"
but, as you note, trying to parse the spaces would be a pain in the ass so I'd rather avoid this option and stick to just the "--key=value" format.

>> That would be have to be compressed.  Why not just have
>> hmc_metric=unit_e?  Why have --algorithm?  This is what I'm
>> missing conceptually in the new scheme.

Okay, let's step back a bit.

A hierarchical structure allows context-specific variables (just like a hierarchical statistical model), which allows us to have many, many possible configurations without forcing the user to worry about specifying irrelevant arguments.  We can, and have in the current implementation, even use the hierarchical structure to prevent the specification of irrelevant arguments -- the code just errs out.

To implement a hierarchy we need to elements: specification of exchangeable levels and specification of child nodes when the options are mutually exclusive.  The latter is accomplished with list arguments that admit one and only one value, while the former is accomplished with categorical arguments.  In particular, to have the full power of a hierarchy we need to allow the value of list arguments to themselves be categorical arguments, so that we choose amongst different possible levels.

As an example, consider choosing a sampling algorithm.

1) We specify that we want to sample instead of optimize or VB or test.
--method=sample

2) Given that we're sampling, we now have a bunch of new options from which to choose.  We specify that we want to use HMC instead of other sampling algorithms
--algorithm=hmc

3) Again, HMC defines new options that are unique to this exact path through the hierarchy.  We specify that we want to use a unit metric
--metric=unit_e

4) And let's use NUTS
--engine=nuts

5) Oh, snap.  NUTS has context-specificy options, too.  Let's open up max_treedepth a bit,
--max_treedepth=12

The full argument string is then

--method=sample --algorithm=hmc --metric=unit_e --engine=nuts --max_treedepth=12

Note that this is a very flexible method.  If we wanted to specify the step size we could do it before or after going down the "engine" subtree.

--method=sample --algorithm=hmc --metric=unit_e --stepsize=0.1 --engine=nuts --max_treedepth=12

or

--method=sample --algorithm=hmc --metric=unit_e --engine=nuts --max_treedepth=12 --stepsize=0.1

Now why can't use a formatting like Bob suggested?  The problem is that it's basically just flattening the hierarchy (which is also something Dan suggested).  Personally, I hate this idea because it makes argument specification a huge pain for the user.  For example, the above specification becomes

sample_algorithm=hmc_metric=unit_e sample_algorithm=hmc_stepsize=0.1 sample_algorithm=engine=nuts --max_treedepth=12

There's far too much typing required of the user, which is not only frustrating but also asking for typos.  And we've only specified a few arguments here!

While it would be great to have a better UI (imagine context-dependent pop-up lists!  What we could do with a web-interface and some javascript…) we're limited to the CLI and we're going to have to make some compromise.  Personally, I believe that users will pick up the current implementation quickly enough and full path specification of each argument is typo- and fatigue-inducing overkill.

But I'm also biased.  :-)

messages.subject: laplace for stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  I've been going thru BDA and I realize that in many of the examples (for instance, Gaussian processes), we recommend Laplace's approximation.  This is what I've been calling the "lmer emulator".  Anyway, I'm realizing how useful it will be to have this in Stan.  The user will just have to write the model and indicate the parameters to be integrated over, and Stan will do the rest.  This could really revolutionize a lot of statistical computing, I think.
A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] laplace for stan
messages.body_plain:
Is labeling parameters more of a computational detail
or is the distinction part of the model?

If it's a computational detail, then I'd rather just list
the parameters in the call to the implementation.  We could
use the names provided by the model to do everything we need,
I think.  It might take another method or two in the model.

If it's something specific to the model, then I'd rather
put it in the model code.   For this, the simplest approach would
be to introduce a "marginalized parameters" block along the same
line as the "parameters" block.  This could also be used for
other nuisance parameters that users don't want to see reported
in the output, which is something we've also been thinking about.

So I guess I'm leaning toward (2).  It'd be nice if the model
was a pure mathematical abstraction, but the reality is that it's
tied to implementation.

- Bob

mdivide_left_spd(A,b) <=> mdivide_left(A,b) where A is a symmetric, positive definite matrix.  It uses the Cholesky factorization to solve the system and has analytic derivatives implemented.

> on the wiki.

The likely reason that this isn't exposed is that I didn't get around to doing the extra leg work of docs, testing, etc.  I implemented it originally to make multi_normal_log faster, although it may not be used now that I've included the quad_form stuff.

>
> > That said, the code Ben provided might actually be a bit slower, depending on the size of Sigma and how many
> > observations there are.  cholesky_decompose and inverse do not have explicit derivatives, so they fall back to the (much

>
> I think the message cutoff before the punchline for this.

What I posted would likely be faster than mdivide_left_tri(cholesky_decompose(...)) for a number of reasons, although they both could be slower than just using multi_normal directly depending on the size of Sigma and the number of observations.

> At the risk of sounding like a mini-Andrew, I'd say we should put this
> kind of discussion in the manual!  Ben and Marcus are the obvious
> candidates for writing this --- I don't think I could manage.

A lot of it will be moot once mult_normal_log is vectorized, so I'm not sure it's worth spending a lot of time and effort on.  Plus, there aren't definitively best practices right now.

Cheers,
Marcus

On 8/9/13 4:35 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> And should something like this be standard too?
>> "adapt -m=5 -e=8 -t=2"
>> That would be the single dash abbreviated form. Spaces wouldn't work here.
>
> The expected standard would be
> "adapt -m 5 -e 8 -t 2"
> but, as you note, trying to parse the spaces would be a pain in the ass so I'd rather avoid this option and stick to just the "--key=value" format.
>
>>> That would be have to be compressed.  Why not just have
>>> hmc_metric=unit_e?  Why have --algorithm?  This is what I'm
>>> missing conceptually in the new scheme.
>
> Okay, let's step back a bit.
>
> A hierarchical structure allows context-specific variables (just like a hierarchical statistical model), which allows us to have many, many possible configurations without forcing the user to worry about specifying irrelevant arguments.  We can, and have in the current implementation, even use the hierarchical structure to prevent the specification of irrelevant arguments -- the code just errs out.

I understand --- but this is what I think is problematic if I'm
understanding properly.  Isn't there a "random" element that
shows up and then defines what the following key-value pairs mean?

> To implement a hierarchy we need to elements: specification of exchangeable levels and specification of child nodes when the options are mutually exclusive.  The latter is accomplished with list arguments that admit one and only one value, while the former is accomplished with categorical arguments.  In particular, to have the full power of a hierarchy we need to allow the value of list arguments to themselves be categorical arguments, so that we choose amongst different possible levels.

But it doesn't have to look like that to the user, as your example
below shows.

> As an example, consider choosing a sampling algorithm.
>
> 1) We specify that we want to sample instead of optimize or VB or test.
> --method=sample
>
> 2) Given that we're sampling, we now have a bunch of new options from which to choose.  We specify that we want to use HMC instead of other sampling algorithms
> --algorithm=hmc
>
> 3) Again, HMC defines new options that are unique to this exact path through the hierarchy.  We specify that we want to use a unit metric
> --metric=unit_e
>
> 4) And let's use NUTS
> --engine=nuts
>
> 5) Oh, snap.  NUTS has context-specificy options, too.  Let's open up max_treedepth a bit,
> --max_treedepth=12
>
> The full argument string is then
>
> --method=sample --algorithm=hmc --metric=unit_e --engine=nuts --max_treedepth=12

This is totally OK by me.  The hierarchy is an implementation detail.

Is this order independent, so that I can put the arguments in any order?

I also don't see any bare arguments like "random" here that change
the meaning of the following parameters.

> Note that this is a very flexible method.  If we wanted to specify the step size we could do it before or after going down the "engine" subtree.
>
> --method=sample --algorithm=hmc --metric=unit_e --stepsize=0.1 --engine=nuts --max_treedepth=12
>
> or
>
> --method=sample --algorithm=hmc --metric=unit_e --engine=nuts --max_treedepth=12 --stepsize=0.1
>
> Now why can't use a formatting like Bob suggested?  The problem is that it's basically just flattening the hierarchy (which is also something Dan suggested).  Personally, I hate this idea because it makes argument specification a huge pain for the user.  For example, the above specification becomes
>
> sample_algorithm=hmc_metric=unit_e sample_algorithm=hmc_stepsize=0.1 sample_algorithm=engine=nuts --max_treedepth=12

I was only suggesting this in the case that something like "stepsize" was ambiguous
between, say, a warmup optimizer and a post-warmup sampler step size, that you use more
specific names.

There are two kinds of pain to users.  One is trying to figure
out some new interface, the other is typing long strings.  Often
the long forms make the figuring out easier and sometimes they
make it harder.

Also, the double equals for algorithm/metric is not standard,
so I certainly wouldn't want to introduce compound arguments.

> There's far too much typing required of the user, which is not only frustrating but also asking for typos.  And we've only specified a few arguments here!
>

> While it would be great to have a better UI (imagine context-dependent pop-up lists!  What we could do with a web-interface and some javascriptï¿½) we're limited to the CLI and we're going to have to make some compromise.  Personally, I believe that users will pick up the current implementation quickly enough and full path specification of each argument is typo- and fatigue-inducing overkill.

I prefer things I can script and read pretty easily.  But I
know opinions vary.

> But I'm also biased.  :-)

So what's the deal with things like "random"?

What I really think we need is more argument lists like the above
in the doc as well as examples of what's not allowed.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> I understand --- but this is what I think is problematic if I'm
> understanding properly.  Isn't there a "random" element that
> shows up and then defines what the following key-value pairs mean?

Yes.  "random" is a categorical argument that defines a new level and key/value pairs within that level.  "hmc", for example, is also a categorical argument that defines a new level and respective key/value pairs.  The difference is that "hmc" is itself defined as a value of a higher argument whereas "random" is not a value.  In other words, "hmc" is one of a mutually-exclusive set whereas "random" is not mutally-exclusive with any other arguments.

> This is totally OK by me.  The hierarchy is an implementation detail.
>
> Is this order independent, so that I can put the arguments in any order?

Yup, the arguments within a level are permutation invariant.

> I also don't see any bare arguments like "random" here that change
> the meaning of the following parameters.

"sample", "hmc", and "nuts" are all categorical variables that define new levels (contexts, meaning, etc).  As noted above, the difference is that they exist as values.  "random" is not derived from any other arguments and instead exists on its own.

>
> Also, the double equals for algorithm/metric is not standard,
> so I certainly wouldn't want to introduce compound arguments.

Exactly.  My point is that if we want categorical arguments that are values to make sense then we have to have bare arguments.

> So what's the deal with things like "random"?

See above.  "random" and "adapt" are not values for other arguments so they appear "bare".

> What I really think we need is more argument lists like the above
> in the doc as well as examples of what's not allowed.

Sure.  Some graphical representations of configurations (with not-included branches of the tree greyed out) would be nice, it just depends on how much detail we'd want to put in.

messages.subject: vectorizing truncated distributions
messages.body_plain:
I just tested the status of vectorization and truncation for
Stan 2.0 and realized we have a problem with models that
get translated into C++ and then fail to compile.    For example,

   data {
     vector<lower=-2,upper=2>[10] y;
   }
   parameters {
     real mu;
   }
   model {
     y ~ normal(mu,1) T[-2,2];
   }

The reason things don't work now is that we currently test
(-2 < y) and (y < 2) and we haven't vectorized the comparison operator.
So it fails to compile in C++.

Here's the calculations we need to make.  Right now they're
being done in the way indicated after the first = sign.  I'd like
to use the new _cdf_log and ccdf_log functions to change that to
the way after the equal sign, which should be more arithmetically
stable and more efficient.

1.  L,U
----------
   log Foo(y|theta) T[L,U];

   = log Foo(y|theta)
     - log [ Foo_cdf(U|theta) - Foo_cdf(L|theta) ]

   = Foo_log(y,theta)
     - log_diff_exp(log Foo_cdf(U|theta),
                    log Foo_cdf(L|theta))

2.  L
------------
   log Foo(y|theta) T[L,]

   = log Foo(y|theta) - log (1 - Foo_cdf(L|theta))

   = log Foo(y|theta) - log Foo_ccdf(L|theta)

3.  U
----------
    log Foo(y|theta) T[,U]

    = log Foo(y|theta) - log Foo_cdf(U|theta)

But vectorization's interaction with truncation is tricky.
Two (overlapping) subcases are easy:

A.  If none of (theta,L,U) are vectorized (but y might be),
all we need to do is use the vectorized Foo_log function and
then multiply the log cdf/ccdf portion of the equation by size(y).

B.  If there is only an L bound or U bound but not both (any
of the other arguments may be vectorized),
then we can just broadcast L up to match y in size and pass
them into the vectorized cdf and ccdf functions.

The tricky case is when we have both L and U and vectorization
in L or U or theta.  If theta weren't an issue, then I'd be
inclined to suggest we just require L and U not to be vectorized.

The only way I can imagine handling this
reasonably is to write functions on a distribution-by-distribution
basis.  What that would mean is that in addition to the following
for each distribution Foo

    Foo_log   log of density function
    Foo_cdf   cumulative distribution function
    Foo_cdf_log  log of cdf
    Foo_ccdf_log log of 1 - cdf

we would also need

    Foo_cdf_diff_log(U,L,theta)

which in the unvectorized case is defined by

    Foo_cdf_diff_log(U,L,theta)

    = log(Foo_cdf(U|theta) - Foo_cdf(L|theta))

    = log_diff_exp(log Foo_cdf(U|theta),
                   log Foo_cdf(L|theta))

Then we can manage the lower AND upper bound case T[L,U] by
just multiplying by any size adjustment needed according to
a simple program

     adjust_size(y,U,L)

which would test that U and L and y have consistent sizes
and return size(y) if U and L are both scalars.

The cdf_diff_log code could be defined using templates
without specialized auto-diff, but using the vector view expression
templates to make the appropriate calls and to cut down on redundant
intermediate calculations (though even the latter isn't a necessity).

It can't be done more generally, even with bind (which I considered),
because we need to know more about the other args and what their
vectorization implications are.

Maybe I'm missing something here and there's an easier way to handle
vectorization of

    y ~ normal(mu,sigma) T[L,U];

where any subset of y, mu, sigma, L, and U may be vectorized.

- Bob

> get translated into C++ and then fail to compile.    For example,
>
>   data {
>     vector<lower=-2,upper=2>[10] y;
>   }
>   parameters {
>     real mu;
>   }
>   model {
>     y ~ normal(mu,1) T[-2,2];
>   }
>
> The reason things don't work now is that we currently test
> (-2 < y) and (y < 2) and we haven't vectorized the comparison operator.
> So it fails to compile in C++.
>
> Here's the calculations we need to make.  Right now they're
> being done in the way indicated after the first = sign.  I'd like
> to use the new _cdf_log and ccdf_log functions to change that to
> the way after the equal sign, which should be more arithmetically
> stable and more efficient.
>
> 1.  L,U
> ----------
>   log Foo(y|theta) T[L,U];
>
>   = log Foo(y|theta)
>     - log [ Foo_cdf(U|theta) - Foo_cdf(L|theta) ]
>
>   = Foo_log(y,theta)
>     - log_diff_exp(log Foo_cdf(U|theta),
>                    log Foo_cdf(L|theta))
>
>
> 2.  L
> ------------
>   log Foo(y|theta) T[L,]
>
>   = log Foo(y|theta) - log (1 - Foo_cdf(L|theta))
>
>   = log Foo(y|theta) - log Foo_ccdf(L|theta)
>
>
> 3.  U
> ----------
>    log Foo(y|theta) T[,U]
>
>    = log Foo(y|theta) - log Foo_cdf(U|theta)
>
>
> But vectorization's interaction with truncation is tricky.
> Two (overlapping) subcases are easy:
>
> A.  If none of (theta,L,U) are vectorized (but y might be),
> all we need to do is use the vectorized Foo_log function and
> then multiply the log cdf/ccdf portion of the equation by size(y).
>
> B.  If there is only an L bound or U bound but not both (any
> of the other arguments may be vectorized),
> then we can just broadcast L up to match y in size and pass
> them into the vectorized cdf and ccdf functions.
>
> The tricky case is when we have both L and U and vectorization
> in L or U or theta.  If theta weren't an issue, then I'd be
> inclined to suggest we just require L and U not to be vectorized.
>
> The only way I can imagine handling this
> reasonably is to write functions on a distribution-by-distribution
> basis.  What that would mean is that in addition to the following
> for each distribution Foo
>
>    Foo_log   log of density function
>    Foo_cdf   cumulative distribution function
>    Foo_cdf_log  log of cdf
>    Foo_ccdf_log log of 1 - cdf
>
> we would also need
>
>    Foo_cdf_diff_log(U,L,theta)
>
> which in the unvectorized case is defined by
>
>    Foo_cdf_diff_log(U,L,theta)
>
>    = log(Foo_cdf(U|theta) - Foo_cdf(L|theta))
>
>    = log_diff_exp(log Foo_cdf(U|theta),
>                   log Foo_cdf(L|theta))
>
> Then we can manage the lower AND upper bound case T[L,U] by
> just multiplying by any size adjustment needed according to
> a simple program
>
>     adjust_size(y,U,L)
>
> which would test that U and L and y have consistent sizes
> and return size(y) if U and L are both scalars.
>
> The cdf_diff_log code could be defined using templates
> without specialized auto-diff, but using the vector view expression
> templates to make the appropriate calls and to cut down on redundant
> intermediate calculations (though even the latter isn't a necessity).
>
> It can't be done more generally, even with bind (which I considered),
> because we need to know more about the other args and what their
> vectorization implications are.
>
> Maybe I'm missing something here and there's an easier way to handle
> vectorization of
>
>    y ~ normal(mu,sigma) T[L,U];
>
> where any subset of y, mu, sigma, L, and U may be vectorized.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: (re)arrangement of code
messages.body_plain:
This email is an extension of conversations I've had with Bob. I'm going through a refactoring of the code base in order to reduce compile times, but I'm blocked on the layout of the code. It's hard to break things out into header / implementation files as-is. Here are some things I want to do (with comments and questions interspersed).

Move stan::agrad to stan::diff
------------------------------------------------------------
This has already been completed. The agrad library has been renamed to diff; namespaces and physical files have been moved appropriately. Could someone review this pull request?
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/pull/175

I've also done a minor cleanup of the headers, but I really focused on moving namespaces.

stan::math and stan::diff: scalar/array/matrix
------------------------------------------------------------
For src/stan/math, src/stan/diff/rev, and src/stan/diff/fwd, we will have 3 folders: scalar, array, and matrix. There will also be a scalar.hpp, array.hpp, and matrix.hpp. That's what should be included if you want a top-level include. So something like:

#include <stan/math/scalar.hpp>

or for reverse mode scalar:

#include <stan/diff/rev/scalar.hpp>

Error handling??
------------------------------------------------------------
Where should error handling go physically? Should there be a folder inside each of the scalar/array/matrix? Like

src/stan/math/{scalar,array,matrix}/error_handling

Or should we put them in:
src/stan/math/error_handling/{scalar,array,matrix}

Or should we put them in:
src/stan/error_handling/{math,diff/rev,diff/fwd}/{scalar,array,matrix}

Traits??
------------------------------------------------------------
Right now, the traits are in src/stan/meta/traits.hpp. All the traits.

We want to break the dependency on autodiff from meta/traits.hpp. So where do we put those? Should we have:
src/stan/meta/traits.hpp
src/stan/meta/diff/rev/traits.hpp
src/stan/meta/diff/fwd/traits.hpp

or:
src/stan/meta/math/traits.hpp
src/stan/meta/diff/rev/traits.hpp
src/stan/meta/diff/fwd/traits.hpp

or:
src/stan/math/traits.hpp
src/stan/diff/rev/traits.hpp
src/stan/diff/fwd/traits.hpp

or something else?

I can also see us breaking apart the traits to individual files, so traits may become a folder with individual metatemplate programs.

I think I could use help with thinking about error_handling and traits. Any thoughts on anything else is appreciated as well. As soon as we have some of these things spec-ed out, I'll add it to the TO-DO list.

On Wednesday, July 31, 2013 12:01:09 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Could you write the correlation matrix version of the three
> cholesky_factor_cov functions in src/stan/prob/transform.hpp?
> These are:
>
>    1.  constrain  (vector + dims to matrix)
>
>    2.  constraint + Jacobian adjust (vector + dims to matrix, increment log prob)
>
>    3.  unconstrain (matrix to vector)

I think the best thing for Stan 2.0 is to use what we have now in transform.hpp for Cholesky factors of correlation matrices, and maybe we'll figure out something with the onion method later. We already have

1. read_corr_L(CPCs, K)
2. read_corr_L(CPCs, K, log_prob)

so I think I just need to add 3. This just entails pulling out the guts of factor_cov_matrix().

> There are examples of the tests I used including error conditions
> in the corresponding test file.
>
> Everything else is just a direct copy of the cholesky_factor_cov case
> that I can knock off in no time.

OK. Do you know the SHAs of the commits that did the cholesky_factor_cov case? Things are harder to find after a feature branch gets deleted.

Another thing that would be good to have for 2.0 is versions of wishart_log() and inv_wishart_log() that take the L such that L * L' is distrubuted accordingly, which will entail another Jacobian adjustment but it is one that we already know. Similarly, a version of lkj_corr() that takes the L such that L * L' is distributed LKJ.

Ben

messages.subject: Warning message issue
messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

So I'm getting a lot of these:

Warning (non-fatal):     sampling statement (~) contains a transformed parameter or local variable.
     You must increment lp__ with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
     Sampling Statement left-hand-side expression:
          row(x_pred,i) ~ normal_log(...)

There are two issues here.  One is that lp__ is deprecated, so the message is somewhat misleading.

The other is that this message isn't correct here, in fact I'm not sure we're really going to be able to provide a warning like this that won't chronically misfire.  I would propose disabling it for now, or providing a flag to stanc which silences it.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Setting Priors on Transforms Parameters
messages.body_plain:
It's very hard to do efficiently.  And I'm not sure how we'd put
it in the language.  But we can compute Jacobians with auto-diff
(just not very efficiently) and also log absolute determinants.

But there's not a good way to recognize triangular Jacobians and
save computation.  Or a good way to separate out which Jacobians
are needed (only variables appearing on left of sampling statements).

In fact, we're going to have to do something like this for the
more sophisticated ODE solvers, where we integrate both the
original equations and their Jacobian (rather than auto-diffing
the integrator itself, which has issues with error bounds on
the Jacobians).

- Bob

print() is configured on develop to only print on
the first iteration.  Does it print on every iteration
in arg_refactor?  If not, I think it should.

This can be controlled by the ostream* argument to log_prob
being set to 0 or to std::cout.   So it's something that needs
to be fixed on the arg_refactor branch rather than on develop.

We discussed this before:

   https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-dev/SMNQIbqnp_8

I don't see any motivation for only doing it once other than
difficulty in determining which iteration is being printed.
I would rather have prints happen on every iteration,
because you may need the debug output for a later
iteration if that's the iteration in which a problem
arises.

- Bob

messages.subject: Possible Language Features
messages.body_plain:
Three questions about the validity of new features -- feel free to split up into separate threads when replying.

1. Prior/Likelihood Blocks

Why did we go with a single model block instead of separate prior/likelihood blocks?  In order to make it easier to code models where the distinction between the two is vague?  For philosophical reasons?

Technically it would be easy to add prior and likelihood blocks (while keeping a model block -- the final log_prob would just be model + prior + likelihood so that prior/likelhood are optional) which would make nested sampling, posterior predictive checks, etc, easier, no?

2. Non-differentiable Functions

I opened a feature request for exposing FFT to the language, and within a few minutes I realized how hard it would be due to the necessary gradients.  But having an FFT for data preprocessing in the "transformed data" block would be extremely useful for many physics applications.

In terms of the language construction, is it difficult to limit functions to the "transformed data" block?

3. Jacobians

Looking through the transformation code, am I correct in assuming that

type_constrain(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& y)

is called whenever transforming, unless the transformation is called within a probability density in which case

type_constrain(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& y, T &lp)

is called?  How does the language identify when a transformation is in the scope of a density?

In any case, right now we force the user to code in the Jacobians by hand but that seems extremely wasteful given that we already have them coded up.  Can we expose

type_constrain(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& y, T &lp)

into the language so that users can just call something like "log_jacobian_uniform(a, b)" to increment using the existing code?  Refactoring all the transformations to isolate the Jacobians from the transformations would be a pain, but even calling "type_constrain" directly and accepting the overhead would probably be worth the ability to avoid coding the Jacobian by hand.

On Sun, Aug 18, 2013 at 2:09 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Three questions about the validity of new features -- feel free to split up into separate threads when replying.
>
> 1. Prior/Likelihood Blocks
>
> Why did we go with a single model block instead of separate prior/likelihood blocks?  In order to make it easier to code models where the distinction between the two is vague?  For philosophical reasons?
>
> Technically it would be easy to add prior and likelihood blocks (while keeping a model block -- the final log_prob would just be model + prior + likelihood so that prior/likelhood are optional) which would make nested sampling, posterior predictive checks, etc, easier, no?

I don't know why the decision was made originally, but in some models the division between likelihood and prior is rather arbitrary.  Also, on a practical level, there can be common terms or calculations between the prior and likelihood which can be shared with everything in one context.  That said, this is a useful distinction that I've been thinking about.  One possible solution I thought of would be to allow named sub-blocks in the model.  E.G., one could do:

model {
  likelihood {
    x ~ normal(mu,sigma);
  }
  prior {
    mu ~ normal(0,1);
    sigma ~ exponential(1);

  }
}

>
> 2. Non-differentiable Functions
>
> I opened a feature request for exposing FFT to the language, and within a few minutes I realized how hard it would be due to the necessary gradients.  But having an FFT for data preprocessing in the "transformed data" block would be extremely useful for many physics applications.
>
> In terms of the language construction, is it difficult to limit functions to the "transformed data" block?

What gradients in FFT are hard?  The FFT is just a linear transform, so its gradient is easy.  The hardest part of the FFT is that Stan has no way to deal with complex numbers right now.

>
> 3. Jacobians
>
> Looking through the transformation code, am I correct in assuming that
>
> type_constrain(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& y)
>
> is called whenever transforming, unless the transformation is called within a probability density in which case
>
> type_constrain(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& y, T &lp)
>
> is called?  How does the language identify when a transformation is in the scope of a density?

The log_prob function has a template parameter which determines whether the volume correction is used.  Optimization doesn't use it, sampling does.  The version without lp is also called for I/O I believe.

>
>
> In any case, right now we force the user to code in the Jacobians by hand but that seems extremely wasteful given that we already have them coded up.  Can we expose
>
> type_constrain(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& y, T &lp)
>
> into the language so that users can just call something like "log_jacobian_uniform(a, b)" to increment using the existing code?  Refactoring all the transformations to isolate the Jacobians from the transformations would be a pain, but even calling "type_constrain" directly and accepting the overhead would probably be worth the ability to avoid coding the Jacobian by hand.

Seems reasonable and easy enough to do, but I'm not sure how useful it would be since if the transformation was correct wouldn't they have just used it directly?  Or is there some use case I'm missing?

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Possible Language Features
messages.body_plain:
> I was thinking more in terms of a single function which computed three values all at once, lp_prior, lp_likelihood and lp_posterior.  lp_posterior would be the sum of the other two plus the volume correction terms and anything that was done in a sub-block.

Sure, but you could just as easily have three wrappers:

prior { return lp_prior + Jacobian correction }
likelihood { return lp_likelihood + Jacobian correction }
posterior { return lp_prior + lp_posterior + Jacobian correction }

> Getting two vectors out and letting users do their own complex manipulations would be more than adequate.
>
> True, but then we'd need the ability to return more than one value from a function which isn't something that's done in the language right now.

Or just return a 2xn matrix.

> But if they defined the distribution on the unconstrained parameters then they don't need the Jacobian.  Alternatively, if they defined the distribution on the constrained parameters then why not just use a constrained definition?

There are lots of complex distributions in physics that are naturally defined on contained parameters.  Yes, you can define them on unconstrained parameters but that is equivalent to computing and coding in the Jacobian.  The idea is to make it much easier for the user by not requiring this additional step.

Oh, I see what you mean.

Warmup and adaptation are two different things.  A warmup period allows the Markov chain to converge to the target distribution -- this is always required of an MCMC method.  In Stan we also take advantage of the warmup period to perform various adaptation routines -- these are not necessary but can be helpful for performance.  Turning adaptation off leaves all algorithmic parameters at their nominal values and just tries to converge to the target distribution.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Multimodality in Unit Vector Transform?
messages.body_plain:
I'm not really talking about mutli-modality persay.  Lets say we use a logit transform to keep parameters in [0,2*pi].  If there is a single dominant mode (on the hypersphere) at 2pi/0 then it will be almost impossible for the sampler to accurately capture this mode with the logit transform because going from 2pi - epsilon to 2pi + epsilon = epsilon will require going from a very large positive number to a very large negative number and the posterior probability in between will be low.

I agree that not using the logit introduces multimodality in the unconstrained space because of the mod 2pi issue.  Thinking about it more, this is likely to screw up adaptation pretty badly because it won't have any finite moments which is perhaps what you're worried about?

Not sure the best solution here.  There are some other parameterizations of unit vectors we could look at perhaps?

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Multimodality in Unit Vector Transform?
messages.body_plain:
Whoa, it's worse than I thought.

In hindsight, it should have been obvious that this would be a problem: S^{1} (the 1 dimensional sphere, or circle) is a manifold without boundary and e no 1-1 mapping to the real line exists.

Without a 1-1 map we'd have to resort to a multi covering, with the obvious choice being a helix.  Indeed, this is what Marcus had previously implemented.  The problem is that he forgot about how densities transform under maps that aren't 1-1 -- you have to include ALL the zeroes.  For the helix, there are an infinite number of zeros and the transformation should read

p(z) = \sum_{i = - infinty}^{infinty} p( \theta(z) + 2 \pi n) | cos( \theta(z) + 2 \pi n ) |

which, to say the least, presents some implementation problems.

Implementing distributions defined on manifolds without boundaries is going to require a different approach.  At this point I would not be against un-exposing the unit vector and von Mises distributions.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Multimodality in Unit Vector Transform?
messages.body_plain:
I don't think it's quite as dire as that.  If you ignore issues related to adaptation, the resulting Markov chain is fine.  Consider it this way:

1. Assume we define the hyperspherical parameters on a limited domain, e.g.., x_\in [0,2pi].  This means we only need one term of that infinite sum, which is what we're doing now.
2. When we do HMC (or MH) there is a question of what to do if the parameter ends up outside of [0,2pi].  One thing we could do is at the end of every step, reset the coordinate modulo 2pi, e.g., x <- mod(x',2pi).  This is fine because we know the mapping is completely invariant to shifts +/- 2pi so nothing changes.  You can think of this another way by assuming that we setup a local chart where y \in [x - pi, x + pi], do the simulation in y, and then go back to the global chart as a representation.
3. Finally, if you never need to do any kind of estimation or diagnostics in x then you never actually need to bother correcting back to [0,2pi] during sampling.

That basically is where things are now.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Multimodality in Unit Vector Transform?
messages.body_plain:
> I don't think it's quite as dire as that.  If you ignore issues related to adaptation, the resulting Markov chain is fine.  Consider it this way:

I disagree.

> 1. Assume we define the hyperspherical parameters on a limited domain, e.g.., x_\in [0,2pi].  This means we only need one term of that infinite sum, which is what we're doing now.

The hyper spherical angles are always defined on [0, 2pi] -- otherwise they wouldn't be hyper spherical angles.  The infinite sum comes when we try to extend [0, 2pi] to \mathcal{R} -- if modular division shows up then an infinite number of terms are required.

> 2. When we do HMC (or MH) there is a question of what to do if the parameter ends up outside of [0,2pi].  One thing we could do is at the end of every step, reset the coordinate modulo 2pi, e.g., x <- mod(x',2pi).  This is fine because we know the mapping is completely invariant to shifts +/- 2pi so nothing changes.  You can think of this another way by assuming that we setup a local chart where y \in [x - pi, x + pi], do the simulation in y, and then go back to the global chart as a representation.

Modular division is not equivalent to an atlas.  In particular, an atlas is assumed to be a minimal covering of charts: for S^{1} that would be two charts, whereas the modular division defines an infinite number of charts. Also, charts can't be defined on [0, 2pi] or (0, 2pi) or (0, 2pi] or [0, 2pi), because the resulting boundary isn't open.

But more importantly if we work in charts then we can't do expectations in the typical fashion.  We have to compute expectations on each chart and then average the results in any overlap using partitions of unity -- not exactly something you'd want to implement.  Essentially, that's what the infinite sum in the change of variables is trying to represent anyways.

> 3. Finally, if you never need to do any kind of estimation or diagnostics in x then you never actually need to bother correcting back to [0,2pi] during sampling.

If adaptation or diagnostics weren't necessary then HMC would have been adopted by everyone a long time ago.  Not exactly realistic example.

messages.body_plain:
I agree with Andrew on this. From the perspective of pure, ideal,
perfect, computation-free posterior inference, there's no distinction
between prior and likelihood, they're just independent terms in the
log-posterior. And we've been talking about a variety of situations
where we'd like to be able to partition the pieces of the
model—besides the PPCs and nested sampling applications mentioned
above, if we eventually want to be able to do stochastic inference
(e.g. contrastive divergence, stochastic EM, stochastic variational
inference) being able to partition the parameters (e.g. into point
estimable and nuisance parameters) would be really helpful.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Multimodality in Unit Vector Transform?
messages.body_plain:
The method of local coordinates is pretty well spelled out in V.4.2 of Hairer et al's book.  In their notation my described use of modular division is finding z_n in Alg 4.5.  All of that aside, if you need to do coherent expectation in the unconstrained space, I agree this is an issue.  Expectation in the constrained space work exactly as expected.

Since the adaption is effectively computing expectation in the unconstrained space it's a potentially big issue, so the question is how to solve it.

As a stop-gap you could do the logit transform but I really dislike what that does to the space.  I think it makes the sampling geometry harder than it needs to be.

Could we do the following to parameterize S^n?

- Let the unconstrained parameters x be a vector in R^n+1
- The mapping to constrained parameters is then y = f(x) = x/norm(x)
- Under the hood place a regularizing distribution on the quantity norm(x) (maybe a inverse gamma or something to keep it away from the singularity at zero).

It would take some effort to work out the volume correction here, but it should be doable as there is a one-to-one mapping between x and (y, norm(x)).

Cheers,
Marcus

On Mon, Aug 19, 2013 at 3:43 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > I don't think it's quite as dire as that.  If you ignore issues related to adaptation, the resulting Markov chain is fine.  Consider it this way:
>
> I disagree.
>
> > 1. Assume we define the hyperspherical parameters on a limited domain, e.g.., x_\in [0,2pi].  This means we only need one term of that infinite sum, which is what we're doing now.
>
> The hyper spherical angles are always defined on [0, 2pi] -- otherwise they wouldn't be hyper spherical angles.  The infinite sum comes when we try to extend [0, 2pi] to \mathcal{R} -- if modular division shows up then an infinite number of terms are required.
>
> > 2. When we do HMC (or MH) there is a question of what to do if the parameter ends up outside of [0,2pi].  One thing we could do is at the end of every step, reset the coordinate modulo 2pi, e.g., x <- mod(x',2pi).  This is fine because we know the mapping is completely invariant to shifts +/- 2pi so nothing changes.  You can think of this another way by assuming that we setup a local chart where y \in [x - pi, x + pi], do the simulation in y, and then go back to the global chart as a representation.
>
> Modular division is not equivalent to an atlas.  In particular, an atlas is assumed to be a minimal covering of charts: for S^{1} that would be two charts, whereas the modular division defines an infinite number of charts. Also, charts can't be defined on [0, 2pi] or (0, 2pi) or (0, 2pi] or [0, 2pi), because the resulting boundary isn't open.
>
> But more importantly if we work in charts then we can't do expectations in the typical fashion.  We have to compute expectations on each chart and then average the results in any overlap using partitions of unity -- not exactly something you'd want to implement.  Essentially, that's what the infinite sum in the change of variables is trying to represent anyways.
>
> > 3. Finally, if you never need to do any kind of estimation or diagnostics in x then you never actually need to bother correcting back to [0,2pi] during sampling.
>
> If adaptation or diagnostics weren't necessary then HMC would have been adopted by everyone a long time ago.  Not exactly realistic example.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Multimodality in Unit Vector Transform?
messages.body_plain:
Actually, I just realized the volume correction isn't too bad.

x is an unconstrained vector in R^n+1
c is a dummy variable which will be fixed to c=1
y is the constrained point on S^n
r is a strictly positive auxiliary variable

Then the transformation is:

f(x,c) = ( c g(x), ||x||^2 )
        = ( y, r )

where g(x) = x/norm(x)

The Jacobian d{y,r}/d{x,c} can be computed (fixing c = 1) and should be full rank so long as x != 0.

In Stan we could add, as part of the log determinant term during transformation, a basic Inverse Gamma prior on r.

Thoughts?  This should preserve the (relatively) nice geometry of S^n in the unconstrained space and not introduce any complications for adaptation.  In fact, the more I think about this, I think it should work better than hyper-spherical coordinates as it has only one singularity at x = 0 which should never actually be hit in practice.

Cheers,
Marcus

I agree that the logit is bad news, but this parameterization is also bad news.  The problem is that there's a scale non-identifiability -- multiply the unconstrained space by a constant and the constrained parameters will still lie on the unit sphere.  Consequently the chain will drift and expectations will remain unreliable.  I don't think there's an immediate answer.  If I have time this week I'll try looking into other implementations of periodic variables.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Multimodality in Unit Vector Transform?
messages.body_plain:
Right, it would be a soft constraint.  I've used similar constructions during optimization and one of the things that turns out is the violation of the constraint (i.e., the magnitude of drift in r) is small unless there is large (i.e., > 90 degree) moves on the sphere in a single step.  This is because the transformation is such that dot(x,df/dx) = 0 where x is the unconstrained parameter and df/dx is the gradient of the objective which only operates on x through the constrained vector y.

All of this is to say that yes, there are potentially some thorny theoretical issues with this approach, but my experience with it in other spaces suggests that they may not show up in practice.

It wouldn't be hard to implement I don't think, although I don't have time to do it myself right now.  Are you working on a model that needs it?

Cheers,
Marcus

>

In fact, the more I think about this, I think it should work better than hyper-spherical coordinates as it has only one singularity at x = 0 which should never actually be hit in practice.

I agree that it would be good to have a normalize() transformation. You've basically described the need for a spherical density, which can be characterized as the product of a uniformally distributed vector on the unit sphere and a random radius with some density appropriate for a non-negative number. But the optimal way to do this with NUTS II would be to put standard normal priors on the elements of x and whatever prior the user wants on the radius. It's less straightforward to think about a prior on y with a Jacobian determinant correction to imply some prior on x and r.

Ben

This is our next big project after 2.0.  We don't think

It's already there for everything but the probability
functions.  So if you write your model by hand, you can
use it now.

> 2) Parameter tagging

Agreed.  This is most general.  This should be pretty easy.

> 3) Prior/Likelihood Identification

Identification how?  As in different functions in the model,
like if theta is the parameters, defining

    log_prior(theta,...)

and

    log_likelihood(theta,...);

so that

    log_prob(theta,...) = log_prior(theta,...) + log_likelihood(theta,...).

I'm not sure we want every model to have these.

If we had statement tagging, we could identify the pieces in
the model, but I don't see how then to expose the different
functions.  Maybe:

    log_sub_prob(TAG,theta,...)

?

difficult.

>
>     Three questions about the validity of new features -- feel free to split up into separate threads when replying.
>
>     1. Prior/Likelihood Blocks
>
>     Why did we go with a single model block instead of separate prior/likelihood blocks?  In order to make it easier to
>     code models where the distinction between the two is vague?  For philosophical reasons?
>
>     Technically it would be easy to add prior and likelihood blocks (while keeping a model block -- the final log_prob
>     would just be model + prior + likelihood so that prior/likelhood are optional) which would make nested sampling,
>     posterior predictive checks, etc, easier, no?
>
>
>
> I don't know why the decision was made originally, but in some models the division between likelihood and prior is
> rather arbitrary.  Also, on a practical level, there can be common terms or calculations between the prior and
> likelihood which can be shared with everything in one context.  That said, this is a useful distinction that I've been
> thinking about.  One possible solution I thought of would be to allow named sub-blocks in the model.  E.G., one could do:
>
> model {
>    likelihood {
>      x ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>    }
>    prior {
>      mu ~ normal(0,1);
>      sigma ~ exponential(1);
>    }
> }

I'd still like a more general way to do this.  Maybe something like
labeling statements:

     @prior
     alpha <- rep(0.0, 10);

     @prior
     theta_raw ~ foo(alpha);

     @likelihood
     theta <- bar(theta_raw);

     @likelihood
     y ~ mulitnomial(theta);

As Michael's pointed out, terms may be shared, so we could do something
like:

     @prior @likelihood
     z <- baz(theta);

>     2. Non-differentiable Functions
>
>     I opened a feature request for exposing FFT to the language, and within a few minutes I realized how hard it would
>     be due to the necessary gradients.  But having an FFT for data preprocessing in the "transformed data" block would
>     be extremely useful for many physics applications.
>
>     In terms of the language construction, is it difficult to limit functions to the "transformed data" block?
>
>
>
> What gradients in FFT are hard?  The FFT is just a linear transform, so its gradient is easy.  The hardest part of the
> FFT is that Stan has no way to deal with complex numbers right now.

If someone can write out the derivatives, it should be easy to
code them up by hand.

But we don't need the complexes if the inputs are all real, do we?

>     3. Jacobians
>
>     Looking through the transformation code, am I correct in assuming that
>
>     type_constrain(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& y)
>
>     is called whenever transforming, unless the transformation is called within a probability density in which case
>
>     type_constrain(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& y, T &lp)
>
>     is called?  How does the language identify when a transformation is in the scope of a density?

> The log_prob function has a template parameter which determines whether the volume correction is used.  Optimization
> doesn't use it, sampling does.  The version without lp is also called for I/O I believe.

No, you still need lp for I/O because we write out lp__.

>     In any case, right now we force the user to code in the Jacobians by hand but that seems extremely wasteful given
>     that we already have them coded up.  Can we expose
>
>     type_constrain(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& y, T &lp)

Absolutely.  It's on the to-do list.

It's no longer trivial because we've deprecated lp__.  So these
somehow need to get ahold of lp__ directly in the same way as
the sampling statements do.  And the same way the RNG need an
implicit RNG.  Shouldn't be too tricky.

>     into the language so that users can just call something like "log_jacobian_uniform(a, b)" to increment using the
>     existing code?  Refactoring all the transformations to isolate the Jacobians from the transformations would be a
>     pain, but even calling "type_constrain" directly and accepting the overhead would probably be worth the ability to
>     avoid coding the Jacobian by hand.
>
>
>
> Seems reasonable and easy enough to do, but I'm not sure how useful it would be since if the transformation was correct
> wouldn't they have just used it directly?  Or is there some use case I'm missing?

That's why it wasn't a high priority to add.  That, and because
it's another sub-case to doc that might confuse users.

- Bob
