messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: lkj_corr_cholesky is not generating Cholesky factors?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: lkj_corr_cholesky is not generating Cholesky factors?
messages.body_plain:
On 8/23/13 12:05 AM, Nicholas Nagle wrote:
>
>     In general, the densities that are used in the model {} block don't imply any restrictions on things in the
>     parameters {} block, but in general the densities typically check whether the restrictions hold. The
>     lkj_corr_cholesky() function doesn't actually check whether the input is lower triangular and that is basically
>     because it was only intended to be used internally but accidentally got exposed to the Stan parser.
>
>
> OK.  Thanks.  So, lkj_corr_cholesky should not be used at this time?

Right.

I don't think we can just Cholesky factor a correlation matrix,
because we won't be accounting for the Jacobian.  It really does
require us to have a correlation Cholesky factor type.

I just filed an issue to remove it from the function signatures for
2.0.

>     What is supposed to happen soon is to introduce a density on L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix with the LKJ
>     density, which is probably what you were expecting.
>
>
> Looking forward to this!  lkj_corr creates non-positive definite matrices too often for comfort and can take a
> relatively long time per iteration.  I was hoping to try out lkj_corr_cholesky, but it sounds like it's not ready.
>
> Again, thanks!

Just a note on what's going on under the hood.

We set things like step sizes to expect a certain amount of
rejection.  As long as it doesn't lead to too strong a correlation
in the output traceplots, it's OK in the sense that the posterior
samples are still drawn properly.

The non-positive definite matrices typically arise from arithmetic
issues in either underflow/overflow, non-transitivity of
addition [ (a + b) + c is not necessarily the same as a + (b + c)
in floating point ], and too large a step size in the Hamiltonian
dynamics simulation (which is intentional to get a good balance
between rejection and movement, just as in Metropolis sampling).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 8/27/13 3:49 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> I reviewed the whole section about the new command line in the manual under feature/arg_refactor branch.  Part of the
> arguments does not make sense to me.

We need to get this at least to the point where you
can understand it or there's no hope for our users.

> I am writing the doc of these arguments for rstan.  I feel bad that I just say
> "please refer to the Stan manual" and I know they are not in the manual of Stan.

Bogus references like that are worse than nothing.

 > So I hope there would be more doc
> about them though some of which should be in the first version of the manual.

Absolutely.  It's on its way.  I'm supposed to be writing some
of it.

> Specifically, I still do not understand the arguments for adaptation, namely, gamma, delta, kappa, t0.  I think we
> should not assume that all users understand dual averaging.

Agreed.

> At least an explanation and a reference in the doc would be
> nice.

I think we need an informal explanation and then a reference.
We don't really want to explain all of dual averaging unless
it's easy.  And then probably only after we explain what we're
doing for HMC and NUTS a bit moe thoroughly.

> Second, the metric option for NUTS.  I do not think NUTS paper talks about geometry much (I might be wrong).

Only implicitly.  You need to read Girolami and Calderhead's RMHMC paper,
or even better, Michael Betancourt's papers.  By geometry, they just
mean the curvature of the posterior (typically measured to second order
through a Hessian).

> So I
> cannot make sense of phrases such as "Geometry of base manifold"

We're using plain old Euclidean geometry so far and the metric's
just Euclidean distance.  RMHMC generalizes this so that Euclidean
geometry's just a special case where the metric (defining distances
between points) is Euclidean.

 > and options unit_e, diag_e, dense_e.

These are the mass matrix shapes, either a unit matrix (usual algebraic
sense of unit for multiplication --- all ones on diagonal), a diagonal
matrix (what we used to call varying step sizes), and a full mass matrix.

Radford's intro to HMC in the MCMC Handbook does a good job explaining
the role of the mass matrix.

> Honestly, I know
> little about manifold and I do not understand the meaning of geometry here, which might be the reason for me.  So I need
> some help.

We should definitely provide a simpler explanation that doesn't depend on
understanding differentiable manifolds and metrics.

>
> Last, I do not know what is "int_time" for HMC.

That's what we used to call step size.  The reason for the new, more
explanatory terminology is that the step size is just the time
interval for the discretization of the Hamiltonian simulation.  The
negative log probability is the potential energy, we provide a random
initial kinetic energy each iteration, and then we trace out the path
given the potential and kinetic energies given the mass matrix.  The
int_time is the time interval for each step of the discrete simulation.

> I read again some previous emails on stan-dev and still cannot
> understand it.  It is of type double, so I guess it is not leapfrog steps that I know is a parameter of HMC.

Right.  Number of steps plus step time determines the overall time of
the simulation.  NUTS figures out the number of steps automatically,
but it should still be settable.

> By the way, I think this part of doc needs another proofread once we settle down on it.

Absolutely --- it's not even a finished draft yet!

- Bob

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I'm all for merging and working from there to make
everyone's life easier.   But let's not ignore anyone's
objections by outvoting them!  Having said that, let's also
not wait forever.  How's that for wishy-washy, namby-pamby,
pass-the-buck, weasel-worded advice?

You might want to rebase it all first, as it looked
like there were a lot of broken intermediate commits.

- Bob

Is it possible to merge in a branch with buggy commits
and then only do bisect on the merge points?  If so,

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] rebasing and bisect
messages.body_plain:
I spent a little bit of time searching for whether we could do that. Unfortunately, it doesn't look like that's how git bisect works by default.

Fortunately, the number of merges due to pull requests is actually low and with the number we have now, I can just walk through and find them and run whatever test on just the merges. And reverting a pull request is easy.

That said, I don't think we should worry about rebasing/squashing the commit history. Although it would be nice if every commit was tested and in a good state, I think our pull request merges into develop are where we can assume and enforce that behavior.

Daniel

messages.subject: memory usage in RStan?
messages.body_plain:
What happens at the end of an RStan run to cause a spike in memory?
Or is this just R allocating space?  I was running some experiments
and tracking the memory just through the system tool and it was under
200MB until it ended and then it shot up to 850MB.  Is this all just
in creating the final object?

For what it's worth, R2jags took 1.7GB for the same model and same number
of iterations (with all other save parameters the same).

Oddly, R2jags, when given the same starting point, looked like it
converged (R-hats all less than 1.05, effective sample sizes all
 > 100), but the answers weren't anywhere near Stan's and had overall
lower log likelihoods.  Stan's answers matched what Sophia got in
Stata, but JAGS's didn't.  Note that this was with R2jags' estimate of
R-hat and n_eff, not Stan's.  I still haven't figured out how to
transfer output from R2jags into RStan.  JAGS was about three times
as fast per iteration, though :-)

- Bob

Thanks for looking into this.  I didn't get the attachment.

I have no idea what R and Mac are up to.  I'm trying to
view memory through the Mac Activity Monitor.  After I
start up the R GUI, but before I run anything, the memory
bounces around between 25MB and 81MB.

Then after calling stan() (which loads the library), memory
goes up to

   100MB

and the C++ compiler uses just under 1GB in
a separate process.  Then after iterations start going, memory
goes to

   160MB

The model has roughly 3K parameters and I'm
running 4 chains of 1000 iterations each, so that's a total of
about 12M values, or about 100MB if you store them as double
objects.  So the memory hit here is consistent with R using
60MB and Stan using 100MB --- that's storing them efficiently!

But now, the second chain has started, and memory usage goes up to

   200MB

So it looks like the memory may be allocated before a chain runs
or after one finishes?  When the third chain starts, that goes up to

   215MB

Then when the fourth chain starts, memory usage goes up to:

   230MB

And then when the fourth chain finishes, memory usage by the R process
as reported by the Activity Monitor goes up to:

   450MB

And that doesn't go back down sitting around for 10 minutes.
Then, running extract() and assigning it takes memory usage up to:

     1GB

- Bob

On Fri, Aug 30, 2013 at 4:54 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Friday, August 30, 2013 4:32:10 PM UTC-4, Ross Boylan wrote:
> > On 8/30/2013 12:54 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > > On Friday, August 30, 2013 2:48:34 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > On 8/30/13 2:17 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> > > > > Here's my current thinking about how to package r/stan.  Comments welcome.
> > > > >
> > > > > The first part of the changes involve stuff that is not Debian-specific, though it may be Unix-specific.  I'll make a
> > > > > configure.ac <http://configure.ac> that looks for the libraries currently used in several places, starting with where they are now in the
> > > > > tarball.  This way they should work fine as things stand now, but they will allow using libraries and headers that are
> > > > > already on the system.
> > > >
> > > > If you change our basic installation procedure, we want to test it
> > > > thoroughly.  What we have now is working pretty well for our use
> > > > cases, and I don't want to add complications that are going to jam
> > > > up our mailing lists with requests for help on installation and
> > > > compatibility with external libraries, versions of Boost and Eigen,
> > > > etc.
> > >
> > > I don't think it is going to be a problem. All that Ross needs is a debian/ folder in STAN_HOME to put stuff to be used in the Debian package. The debian folder is just text files and is pretty small, so we could just put that into main repo or we can create a debian branch off of each future released version of Stan.
> > Debian has a notion of the original source, i.e., the upstream source.  In this case it will require some changes to omit the external libraries, which will make it a "repackaged" original source.  Although technically all other changes go under debian/, those changes include patches that get applied to the larger tree.
>
> We can make the debian/ folder part of the original source if you like. Or you can uncompress a stan_debian.tar.gz over the original source to add the debian/ folder. Whatever is easiest for you.
>
> > > I think what Ross proposes is about right, although the details might have to change. Here are the packages derived from the Stan source I think:
> > > libstan (build-depends on large parts of boost-1.54 and libeigen3)
> > > libstanc (build-depends on small parts of boost-1.54 and libstan)
> > What's the difference between libstan and libstanc?
>
> libstan basically just deals with math. In principle, one can write a C++ file by hand that links to libstan, although we aren't aware of anyone actually doing so yet. libstanc is something that stanc needs to parse a .stan file to a C++ file. What has never been clear to me is why libstanc depends on libstan but it does in the makefile for some reason.
>

That's probably my doing from before I knew how to really control make. If we can, we should probably split out the dependency. Although, it does make some sense to have the libstan library built when the compiler is built so it's available for use immediately.

> > I thought the libraries, meaning files named .so, .dll, or .a (i.e., not R libraries) was limited to
> > the main stan libraries
>
> I've got this under STAN_HOME/
>
> goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ ls -l -h bin/
> total 104M
> -rw-r--r-- 1 goodrich goodrich 1.4M Aug 30 15:24 libstan.a
> -rw-r--r-- 1 goodrich goodrich  80M Aug 30 15:24 libstanc.a
> -rwxr-xr-x 1 goodrich goodrich 899K Aug 30 15:24 print
> drwxr-xr-x 6 goodrich goodrich 4.0K Aug 30 15:22 stan
> -rwxr-xr-x 1 goodrich goodrich  22M Aug 30 15:26 stanc
>
> so there are two "main" Stan libraries: libstan.a and libstanc.a. Plus the print and stanc executables.
>

messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, 31 August 2013 08:28:49 UTC+1, Andrew Gelman  wrote:
> Hi all.  Would this paper by Chunyi Wang and Radford Neal be helpful for us?
>
> http://www.cs.utoronto.ca/~radford/ftp/gp-approx.pdf
>
> A

At first glance the analysis seems naïve. You don't have to calculate the cholesky factors each time you calculate the posterior, it is constant for a given set of observations.

I also note the GP does not include any kind of polynomial term, which is vital in many cases.

Depending on different dimensions, it is also incorrect to assume cholesky back substitution dominates. It certainly doesn't in my case.

finally, of course, there is the issue of calculating derivatives for use in hamiltonian methods. This is a little tricky if, as in my case, the posterior depends on the variance, and the covariance function is, for example, a Matern function.

In practice, constructing the k matrix (eq. 25) can easily dominate in high dimensions. In my situation, I can for example have 200 dimensions and 100 observations.
